c.tagline: Ivory Coast's serene political capital, home to the world's largest basilica

taxi.fareNote: Shared woro-woro taxis run fixed routes for small flat fares; individual chartered taxis should have the fare agreed before departure, as meters are rare.

emergency.note: Emergency response can be slow outside the main hospital; the Yamoussoukro University Hospital Center (CHR) is the primary referral facility.

hood_landmark.Millionnaire: Basilica of Our Lady of Peace

avoid.reason: Petty theft can occur around the markets and quiet streets after dark, so avoid walking alone at night and keep valuables out of sight.

hood_desc: The city's showpiece district, built around the immense Basilica of Our Lady of Peace, a near-replica of St. Peter's in Rome commissioned by President Houphouët-Boigny.
The administrative heart of the city, home to government ministries, the Presidential Palace, and its famous lake of sacred crocodiles.
A planned residential district near the Félix Houphouët-Boigny Foundation golf course, quieter and greener than the city center.
An older, predominantly Muslim trading quarter with a lively market and the Grand Mosque, reflecting the city's northern Ivorian trade links.
A busy commercial and residential neighborhood centered on Yamoussoukro's main market, with small bars, eateries, and everyday shops.

water.note: Drink bottled or filtered water only.

transit.hours: Informal transit runs roughly dawn to 9-10pm, with limited service after dark
transit.pay: Cash fares paid directly to the driver at fixed low rates per route
transit.map: No official transit map; routes are learned locally or from drivers
transit.note: There is no formal transit authority; the city's wide boulevards mean much travel is by private car or taxi

air: Yamoussoukro Airport (ASK), domestic flights to Abidjan
train: No passenger rail service currently operating
bus: Intercity coaches (UTB, MTT) connect to Abidjan (~2.5-3 hrs), Bouaké, and other cities

tip.r: Tipping isn't customary, but rounding up or leaving small change for good service is welcomed, especially at hotels and restaurants used by visitors.

food.name: Attieke with poisson braise
food.desc: Fermented cassava couscous served with whole fish grilled over charcoal and smothered in onion, tomato and chilli. The national plate of Cote d'Ivoire.

places.name: Attieke Poisson Chez Sandrine
places.note: Built around exactly this pairing; fresh fish grilled to order in the Ivorian way.

places.name: Poisson Braise Chez Gisele
places.note: Local specialist in grilled fish, a reliable evening maquis for attieke plates.

places.name: Restaurant La Djiboua
places.note: Known for careful preparation of attieke and grilled fish rather than tourist menus.

food.name: Kedjenou
food.desc: Chicken or guinea fowl sealed in a clay canari with tomato, ginger and chilli and steamed in its own juices, shaken not stirred. Baoule country's signature.

places.name: Maquis Restaurant Chez Tantie Amoin
places.note: Traditional maquis cooking; the place to ask for kedjenou de poulet.

places.name: Maquis Bon-Choix
places.note: Long-standing local maquis serving the Ivorian classics with attieke or rice.

places.name: Restaurant La Djiboua
places.note: Hub of traditional Ivorian dishes including slow-steamed kedjenou.

food.name: Foutou banane with sauce graine
food.desc: Pounded plantain and cassava dough eaten by hand with sauce graine, the thick palm-nut sauce cooked with smoked fish, crab or beef.

places.name: Maquis Restaurant Chez Tantie Amoin
places.note: Foutou pounded fresh and served with palm-nut or groundnut sauce.

places.name: Maquis 106
places.note: Authentic maquis menu covering foutou and the heavy village sauces.

places.name: Grand Marche de Yamoussoukro
places.note: Market cookshops serve foutou and sauce at midday for market traders.

food.name: Poulet braise
food.desc: Chicken flattened, marinated and grilled over wood, then brushed with onion and tomato sauce. Eaten with attieke or alloco under the maquis awnings.

places.name: Maquis Bon-Choix
places.note: Charcoal-grilled chicken with attieke, the standard maquis order.

places.name: Yakro Sur Seine
places.note: Riverside maquis with generous portions of grilled chicken and fish.

places.name: Maquis 106
places.note: Evening grill house where locals gather for braised chicken and beer.

food.name: Alloco
food.desc: Ripe plantain fried in palm oil until dark and sweet, served with raw onion and pepper sauce and often a fried egg. The street snack of every corner.

places.name: Grand Marche de Yamoussoukro
places.note: Alloco women fry plantain all afternoon around the market lanes.

places.name: Attieke Poisson Chez Sandrine
places.note: Alloco served as the side to grilled fish and chicken.

places.name: Yakro Sur Seine
places.note: Riverside spot where alloco arrives with the grilled dishes.

food.name: Garba
food.desc: The cheapest street meal in the country: attieke topped with chunks of deep-fried tuna, raw onion, tomato and searing pepper, wrapped in paper.

places.name: Grand Marche de Yamoussoukro
places.note: Garba kiosks around the market and lorry park serve from morning to night.

places.name: Garba kiosks, Quartier Habitat
places.note: Neighbourhood garbadromes feeding students and workers for pocket change.

places.name: Maquis 106
places.note: Sit-down alternative if you would rather eat fried fish and attieke at a table.

food.name: Bangui (palm wine)
food.desc: Fresh palm sap tapped in the surrounding villages, milky and lightly fizzy in the morning, sharper and stronger by evening. Distilled it becomes koutoukou.

places.name: Grand Marche de Yamoussoukro
places.note: Sellers bring in jerrycans of fresh bangui from the surrounding Baoule villages.

places.name: Maquis Restaurant Chez Tantie Amoin
places.note: Traditional maquis where palm wine is drunk with kedjenou and foutou.

places.name: Roadside bars, route de Bouafle
places.note: Village tapping country; roadside stands sell bangui by the bottle.

food.name: Bissap and gnamankoudji
food.desc: Chilled hibiscus infusion and fiery fresh ginger juice, both sold in frozen sachets or bottles. The everyday non-alcoholic drinks of Ivorian streets.

places.name: Grand Marche de Yamoussoukro
places.note: Vendors sell frozen bissap and ginger sachets from cool boxes all day.

places.name: Attieke Poisson Chez Sandrine
places.note: Homemade juices served cold with the grilled fish.

places.name: Maquis Bon-Choix
places.note: Keeps bissap and ginger alongside the beers for non-drinkers.

landmarks: Basilica of Our Lady of Peace
The largest church on Earth, a marble-and-stained-glass colossus modeled on St. Peter's, rising surreally from the Ivorian savanna.
Presidential Palace & Sacred Crocodile Lake
Crocodiles prowl the moat of Houphouët-Boigny's vast palace; glimpsing the legendary reptiles along the perimeter fence is Yamoussoukro's strangest spectacle.
Grand Mosque of Yamoussoukro
An elegant twin-minaret mosque near the palace quarter, testament to the founding president's vision of interfaith harmony in his hometown capital.
Fondation Félix Houphouët-Boigny
A monumental marble congress center dedicated to peace research, its vast halls and manicured gardens honoring Côte d'Ivoire's first president.
Saint Augustin Cathedral
The city's striking earlier cathedral, a bold modernist church that served the faithful before the great basilica rose across town.
Hôtel Président
A landmark 1970s tower hotel whose panoramic top-floor restaurant offers the best aerial view of the basilica and the capital's grand boulevards.
Yamoussoukro's Artificial Lakes
A chain of crocodile-inhabited lakes threads the city's oversized avenues, lending the planned capital its languid, water-laced character at sunset.
Kossou Dam & Lake Kossou
An hour away, this vast hydroelectric reservoir on the Bandama River offers fishing villages, rich birdlife and sweeping inland-sea horizons.
Abokouamekro Game Reserve
A day-trip savanna reserve stocked with rhinos, buffalo and antelope, created under Houphouët-Boigny to bring safari country to the capital's doorstep.
INP-HB (Félix Houphouët-Boigny National Polytechnic Institute)
West Africa's flagship polytechnic campus, whose sweeping modernist architecture embodies the president's dream of an Ivorian city of knowledge.

train.note: Yamoussoukro has no railway station. The country's only line, the metre-gauge Abidjan-Ouagadougou railway operated by Sitarail, runs east of the city through Agboville, Dimbokro, Bouaké and Ferkessédougou to Burkina Faso; the nearest stations are Dimbokro roughly 90 km east and Bouaké about 100 km north. Passenger service on the line is limited and irregular and has been repeatedly interrupted by infrastructure problems, including the 2016 collapse of the N'Zi river bridge, so it is not a dependable option. Practically everyone travels to Yamoussoukro by coach or car.

intl.to: Ouagadougou & Bobo-Dioulasso (Burkina Faso), Bamako (Mali) and Accra (Ghana) - through coaches calling at Yamoussoukro or connecting at Abidjan and Bouaké
intl.op: UTB and other Ivorian coach companies — tickets at the Yamoussoukro gare routière

bus.note: Yamoussoukro lies on the main A3 highway 240 km north-west of Abidjan, so it is well served by the coaches running between the coast and the interior; they use the gare routière on the edge of the centre and tickets are bought at the company kiosks in cash on the day. UTB is the best-known Ivorian operator on the Abidjan-Bouaké-Ferkessédougou corridor, with Abidjan taking about 3 hr 30 min to 4 hours on the motorway and Bouaké around 1 hr 30 min. For Burkina Faso and Mali most services originate in Abidjan and pick up here or at Bouaké; expect a long night run, several police checkpoints and a border stop where passports and yellow fever certificates are checked. ECOWAS nationals cross freely, but other travellers need visas arranged in advance.

ferry.note: Yamoussoukro is 240 km inland from the Atlantic and has no port; nearby Lake Kossou is crossed only by local pirogues serving lakeside villages, with no scheduled passenger boat service.

half.name: Bouaké
half.blurb: Ivory Coast's second-largest city, a regional trading hub north of Yamoussoukro along the main highway.

full.name: Abidjan
full.blurb: Ivory Coast's economic capital and largest city, with a lagoon-side skyline, markets, and the Plateau business district.
